params.question: According to the ICMR-NIN 2020 guidelines, the approximate daily energy requirement for a child aged one to three years is:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is too low even for a one-year-old. An infant aged 6–12 months already needs about 98 kcal/kg/day, which totals more than 800 kcal for most infants.
Correct. The ICMR-NIN 2020 guideline recommends approximately 1000 kcal/day for children aged 1–3 years, rising to about 1350 for 4–6 year-olds and 1690 for 7–9 year-olds.
This is the ICMR-NIN 2020 recommendation for a 4–6-year-old child, not for the 1–3-year age group.
This figure corresponds to the requirement for a 7–9-year-old child. Energy needs rise with age, and each age bracket has a distinct benchmark.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the ICMR-NIN 2020 energy ladder: 1000 kcal/day at 1–3 years → 1350 at 4–6 → 1690 at 7–9 → 2190 (boys) or 1970 (girls) at 10–12 → up to 2640 in adolescent boys.
Well done. Knowing the age-specific energy benchmarks is the first step toward spotting a dietary gap and planning an appropriate diet.

params.question: A community health worker needs to screen children for acute malnutrition in a village without access to growth charts or a calibrated scale. Which anthropometric measurement is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Weight-for-age requires both a calibrated scale and a growth chart for interpretation, making it impractical for the scenario described.
Correct. MUAC needs only a simple measuring tape and uses fixed cutoffs — below 11.5 cm indicates SAM, 11.5–12.5 cm indicates MAM — so no growth chart is needed for interpretation.
Head circumference tracks brain growth in the first two years of life, not acute nutritional status. It also requires a reference chart to interpret.
Skinfold measurement requires callipers and trained technique, and is used mainly in research settings — not suitable for routine community screening.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: MUAC stands out because it needs no growth chart and no scale. Its fixed cutoffs (< 11.5 cm = SAM, 11.5–12.5 cm = MAM) allow instant classification in the field.
Exactly. MUAC's simplicity and fixed cutoffs make it the go-to screening tool in community settings where scales and charts are unavailable.

interactions.label: Which clinical feature is the single defining criterion that separates kwashiork

params.question: Which clinical feature is the single defining criterion that separates kwashiorkor from marasmus in a child with severe acute malnutrition?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Severe wasting is the hallmark of marasmus, not kwashiorkor. In kwashiorkor, oedema may actually mask the degree of underlying wasting.

Correct. Bilateral pitting oedema is the defining feature of kwashiorkor. It can extend upward to cause a swollen, moon-shaped face. When severe wasting and oedema coexist, the classification becomes marasmic-kwashiorkor.
While apathy and anorexia are typical of kwashiorkor, they are not the defining criterion. A child with marasmus can also be lethargic if severely unwell. Oedema is what makes the classification.

answers.text: Thin, discoloured hair that pulls out easily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hair changes (flag sign) are seen in kwashiorkor but are not the defining criterion. Hair changes can also occur in other micronutrient deficiencies. Bilateral pitting oedema is what formally distinguishes kwashiorkor.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the classification rule: no oedema + severe wasting = marasmus; bilateral pitting oedema = kwashiorkor; both together = marasmic-kwashiorkor. Oedema is the single feature that shifts the classification.

Right. Bilateral pitting oedema is the WHO's defining criterion for kwashiorkor. Its presence with severe wasting classifies the child as marasmic-kwashiorkor, which carries the highest mortality risk.

interactions.label: Adolescent girls require approximately 21 mg of iron daily, nearly twice the rec

params.question: Adolescent girls require approximately 21 mg of iron daily, nearly twice the recommendation for boys of the same age. Which physiological factor best explains this difference?

answers.text: Girls undergo a faster linear growth spurt than boys

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Boys actually have a more prolonged growth spurt and accumulate more muscle mass. The greater iron need in girls is not driven by growth velocity.

answers.text: Girls deposit more iron into rapidly growing bone tissue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Calcium, not iron, is the mineral primarily deposited in bone during peak bone building. The iron difference has a different explanation.

answers.text: Menstrual blood loss creates a recurring iron drain that boys do not experience

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Once menstruation begins, girls lose iron cyclically, raising their daily requirement to about 21 mg/day. This is compounded by the poor bioavailability of iron from plant-based Indian diets, making iron-deficiency anaemia very common.

answers.text: Girls have higher basal metabolic rates during puberty

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Boys actually develop higher basal metabolic rates after puberty because they build more lean muscle mass. The iron gap is related to menstrual losses, not metabolic rate.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical point: menstruation creates a recurring iron loss that boys simply do not have. At 21 mg/day, the recommendation for adolescent girls is nearly double the 11–15 mg/day for boys — and even this is hard to meet on a purely vegetarian Indian diet.

Exactly. Menstrual losses are the key driver. Combined with poor iron absorption from predominantly plant-based Indian diets, this makes iron-deficiency anaemia one of the most prevalent nutritional problems in adolescent girls.

interactions.label: During examination of an obese 14-year-old boy, you notice purple striae on his

params.question: During examination of an obese 14-year-old boy, you notice purple striae on his abdomen alongside truncal obesity. Silver-white striae are present on his thighs. What is the most appropriate clinical interpretation?

answers.text: Both types of striae are benign stretch marks from rapid weight gain and need no further investigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Silver-white striae are indeed benign in simple obesity, but purple striae have a different clinical significance that should not be dismissed.

answers.text: Purple striae suggest possible Cushing syndrome and warrant further endocrine evaluation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Purple striae indicate active collagen breakdown from cortisol excess, raising suspicion for Cushing syndrome — a secondary cause of obesity. Silver-white striae, by contrast, result from simple skin stretching in rapid weight gain.

answers.text: Purple striae indicate insulin resistance, similar to acanthosis nigricans

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acanthosis nigricans — the velvety brown thickening of skin at the neck and axillae — is the marker of insulin resistance. Purple striae point toward cortisol excess, an entirely different pathological pathway.

answers.text: The colour difference reflects the age of the striae; purple ones are recent and will turn white over time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While striae do lighten with age, the clinical teaching here is that purple striae in an obese child should specifically prompt investigation for Cushing syndrome — they are not merely a stage in the natural fading process.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the colour rule for striae in an obese child: silver-white = simple stretching from weight gain (benign); purple = active cortisol-driven collagen breakdown, pointing toward Cushing syndrome and requiring endocrine work-up.
Well spotted. Distinguishing purple from silver-white striae during the obesity examination is a key step in separating simple primary obesity from secondary causes like Cushing syndrome.
